sources.title: God of War: Laufey Release Date Delayed
sources.text: A new announcement confirms that God of War: Laufey’s release date has been delayed by over three months, now arriving in May 2027. Santa Monica Studio announced the game’s pre-order bonuses and game editions in September 2026, with the release date still sticking to what was revealed during San Diego Comic-Con 2026 in July, which was set for February 2027. However, for some reason, the developers will need to push that date back by over three months. A new post by Santa Monica Studios’ official X account (formerly Twitter) confirms that God of War: Laufey’s release has been delayed. The new date has been set as May 20, 2027. The developers have stated that they don’t take the excitement players have shown for granted and want to make the “most of each moment” until release to provide the finishing touches and bring the game “to its fullest potential”. God of War: Laufey is the next big exclusive from PlayStation and the next chapter in the beloved God of War franchise. For the first time in the series, players follow the story of a character other than Kratos, and it’s none other than Faye, his wife, since the character entered Norse mythology. The new story sees Faye awaken in a strange land after her death, and to save Kratos and Atreus, she must fight gods in the afterlife in a place known as Everywhen. There are a lot of ruthless gods with dangerous magic to fighting against, but Faye is also a warrior that doesn’t back down from a fight. God of War: Laufey is a PS5 exclusive title. What are your thoughts on God of War: Laufey’s release date being delayed? Leave your thoughts down in the comments, and join the official Insider Gaming Discord server . Laufey stars Faye, the wife of usual God of War protagonist Kratos, and she is played again by Deborah Ann Woll. Based on a 23-minute gameplay reveal earlier this year , Laufey looks to play differently than the other recent God of War games, with more of a focus on acrobatic action.

sources.title: God of War Laufey Hit With Big Delay
sources.text: Sony Santa Monica's spinoff slides out of February 2027 Sony Santa Monica has announced it has made the decision to delay God of War Laufey . The upcoming spinoff game of the iconic PlayStation series was initially slated to be released next February, but players will now have to wait a few extra months to get their hands on it. The studio has set a new release date for the PlayStation 5 exclusive, pushing the game to May 2027. Son's Santa Monica Studio made the announcement in a statement on X , explaining that it will use the extra time to push the game to its fullest potential. Here's the studio's full message: Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we’ve been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye’s journey through the Everywhen. We don’t take for granted the trust placed in our studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans. With this in mind, we’ve made the decision to delay God of War Laufey’s release to May 20th, 2027. We will make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential. On behalf of everyone on the team, we appreciate your patience and we’ll be back to share more updates soon! Laufey stars Deborah Ann Woll in the titular role, the wife of longtime series protagonist Kratos. Faye (as she is referred to) was first introduced in God of War (2018), which begins with her funeral, but players never actually met her until 2022's God of War Ragnarök , in which Woll first portrayed her. Laufey was officially revealed during this year's June State of Play after months of rumors about its existence. If you are asking yourself how Faye could be the protagonist of a game when she died in God of War (2018), then don't worry, Sony Santa Monica has an answer. Laufey will take place concurrently with the 2018 soft reboot and its sequel, showing the character's own adventure. It will take her to the Everywhen, an afterlife for the gods, in which she will attempt to help Kratos and their son Atreus from beyond the grave. Woll will be joined by Jack Quaid as Phranque (a talking cube), Perlina Lau as Rue, and Christopher Judge back again as Kratos. Considering this is Faye's story, Kratos will likely only have a minor role. Laufey will also be a bit of a mechanical departure for the series. While it is still going to be an action-forward affair, Faye's combat is much more acrobatic and evokes Devil May Cry . Faye also has the ability to punch people so hard that their souls leave their bodies (kind of like that scene in Doctor Strange ). It is clear that Faye will be just as powerful and dangerous as her husband. While Sony Santa Monica is developing Laufey , it has also confirmed that a new mainline game in the series led by Kratos is in development . Amazon is also currently developing a live-action adaptation of the 2018 soft reboot, with Dave Bautista set to star as Kratos. God of War Laufey will be released on May 20, 2027 on PlayStation 5.

sources.title: God of War Laufey delayed three months to May 2027, as Sony Santa Monica escapes a packed February
sources.text: "We will make the most of each moment until then." God of War Laufey has been delayed. Sony Santa Monica's PS5 exclusive is now dodging the crowded month of February and will instead come out on 20th May, 2027. Developer Sony Santa Monica announced it's pushing back the upcoming action epic via a brief social media post . While the studio stopped short of giving a reason for the delay, it did say it's using the extra time to polish Faye's solo adventure. "Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we've been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye's journey through the Everywhen. We don't take for granted the trust placed in the studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans," the studio wrote. "With this in mind, we've made the decision to delay God of War Laufey's release to May 20th, 2027," the statement continued. "We will make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential. On behalf of everyone on the team, we appreciate your patience and we'll be back to share more updates soon." God of War Laufey is notably the first game in the famed PlayStation series to not star Kratos in the lead role. This time around, Faye takes the lead through a version of the afterlife that houses gods and deities from multiple mythologies - and it's bringing back the original series' faster combat , too. Of course, Kratos will return in future God of War games (he also shows up here and there during Faye's romp), and whatever that next Kratos game becomes, it'll supposedly connect to the events of Laufey , according to the developer. On the bright side, the delay might be good news for anyone worried about their impossibly large and ever expanding backlogs. February 2027 is already packed with really exciting games - from the Fable reboot and Persona 4 Revival to Metro 2039. Hopefully, Laufey's delay gives everyone more breathing room.

sources.text: A Santa Monica Studio anunciou de surpresa na tarde desta quarta-feira (04) que God of War Laufey , novo exclusivo de PS5, teve seu lançamento adiado. Antes previsto para chegar em 16 de fevereiro de 2027, o jogo agora será lançado em 20 de maio de 2027 . Em comunicado, o estúdio californiano explicou que precisa de mais tempo para concluir o desenvolvimento e aproveitar o potencial do projeto. O anúncio foi acompanhado de uma mensagem de agradecimento aos fãs pela expectativa e pelo apoio desde a revelação do game, que ocorreu no State of Play de junho . Nas redes sociais, a Santa Monica afirma que a decisão foi tomada para garantir que God of War Laufey alcance o resultado esperado pela equipe. Com isso, o lançamento acabou sendo postergado em pouco mais de três meses. “Desde a revelação de God of War Laufey em junho, estamos profundamente gratos por ver tanto entusiasmo pela jornada de Faye pelo Mundo Infinito”, declarou o estúdio. A empresa também destacou a importância da confiança dos fãs no desenvolvimento do projeto. “Não consideramos como garantida a confiança depositada no estúdio para criar uma experiência extraordinária, à altura da paixão e dedicação de nossos fãs”, acrescentou. Por fim, a equipe afirmou que utilizará o período adicional para finalizar o jogo e explorar todo o seu potencial. “Aproveitaremos ao máximo cada momento até lá, dando os retoques finais e explorando todo o potencial do jogo”, concluiu a mensagem. Revelado em junho no State of Play, God of War Laufey será o primeiro jogo principal da franquia a colocar uma protagonista diferente de Kratos no centro da aventura. Aqui, os jogadores controlarão Faye, esposa do protagonista, que retorna dos mortos em uma jornada além da vida. A história começa quando a personagem desperta em uma terra desconhecida após seu próprio funeral. Ao perceber que seus planos para proteger Kratos e Atreus estão ameaçados, ela precisa enfrentar diferentes divindades no Todo-Tempo, um reino onde deuses de várias mitologias disputam poder. O gameplay com mais de 20 minutos divulgado pelo estúdio no evento da Sony apresentou trechos de combate contra duas divindades — possivelmente Sekhmet, da mitologia egípcia, e Begtse, associada à mitologia tibetana . O cenário promete reunir referências de diferentes tradições mitológicas. Além disso, Deborah Ann Woll retorna ao papel de Faye após sua participação em God of War Ragnarok . Segundo a Santa Monica, a proposta é combinar “o movimento e a fluidez da era grega com a abordagem da era nórdica à construção de mundos”, mas mantendo os elementos característicos que consagraram o momento atual da saga. Aos ansiosos por mais aventuras pela saga nórdica, saiba que a PlayStation já abriu a pré-venda de God of War Laufey . Como de costume, o spin-off será vendido em duas edições: Edição Standard e Edição Digital Deluxe — que inclui conteúdos adicionais para personalizar a experiência. A Edição Standard de God of War Laufey estará disponível tanto em formato digital quanto físico . Já a Edição Digital Deluxe será exclusiva do formato digital e adicionará os seguintes extras na edição: Além disso, aqueles que realizarem a pré-encomenda de qualquer uma das edições de God of War Laufey antes do lançamento ainda receberão bônus — incluindo o conjunto de armadura Último Desejo, a aparência Folhas Douradas de Phranque e um pacote de recursos extras para a aventura. sources.title: Eight years ago the idea of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel had me captivated, but can Bethesda recapture the magic?
sources.text: Eight years ago, I sat at my desk enthralled. Bethesda had just released the first trailer for The Elder Scrolls 6 , a then mysteriously nameless, locationless sequel to one of the biggest games of all time, and I reckoned I'd just found the secrets to both. It was going to be set in the region of Hammerfell, I reckoned . And the city of Sentinel was a crucial factor in reasoning why. Admittedly, I'm maybe a little more horrified at my level of Elder Scrolls obsession than I am chuffed at any apparent clairvoyance. Ultimately it was a bit of a punt, launched off the back of a day's worth of fanatical hyperfocus and exactly the right amount of the old Gamer Network office's weapons-grade filter coffee. "There's not really a lot to go on here", I wrote, sagely, "but, if we had to, we'd plant our flag in Hammerfell as the location of The Elder Scrolls 6 ." Indulge me a bit and let's retread the reasoning. First, three assumptions were required in order to make any kind of guess at all: The Elder Scrolls 6 would not be set in all of Tamriel; not set outside of Tamriel; and would be set somewhere vaguely close in the timeline to the events of Morrowind , Oblivion and Skyrim - so as to make that bit of scrabbly rock and ruined castle, visible in that now infamous first teaser, at least somewhat traceable with contemporary descriptions in the lore. Then came a lot of narrowing down. Not Morrowind, Cyrodiil, Skyrim or the Summerset Isles, I decided, as we'd been to all of those too recently (I'll leave it up to you whether another eight years since Morrowind lets that one still count as remotely "recent", but still). And then not Valenwood, Elsweyr, or Black Marsh, thanks to the topography of the land in the trailer and the type of environment on show. That left High Rock and Hammerfell, the former of which we ruled out because of its relative size - on the small side for a presumably beefy new TES game - and more importantly, the architecture that seemed at odds with the sandy stone just barely visible in the structures of that first teaser. And finally: Sentinel. The city was perfectly positioned - along a coast with the sea to the right, dry mountains in the foreground, warm stone ruins to the left, no visible land beyond. Now, that setting is all but confirmed - "all but" as, technically , nothing's set in stone yet, pardon the pun. All we've since been shown is a sand dune, an Elder Scroll, the name Sentinel, and a brief quote from a Moth Priest to a Hammerfell High Queen. But we can pretty much lock it in. To the Elder Scrolls obsessive who spent that day eight years ago scurrying down endless YouTube rabbit holes and lingering on the dustiest unofficial wiki pages, the thought of a game set there ought to be tantalising. Already, even with that paper thin new teaser, there's enough to start picking at. The new trailer's quote is dated just four years after the events of Skyrim, for instance, with both that territory and Cyrodiil located right next door, making for some lovely opportunities for crossovers and references to wider events. And the quote itself is curious. As our guides team have already speculated , the notion of "A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate" gives off the faintest whiff of a time-forking Dragon Break. That being the timeline-branching, multiple-player-choice-enabling thing that happened at the end of The Elder Scrolls 2: Daggerfall, a game which took place - aha! - in the Iliac Bay between High Rock and Hammerfell. Surely, the same bay we're looking at in that original TES 6 trailer. It keeps going! The "victory" mentioned in that quote could refer to the victory won by the people of Hammerfell against a Thalmor invasion, in a conflict that - ooh! - took place around the same time Skyrim's main story was happening, and just a few years before that quote is dated. Could we get branching timelines? A tying together of the overarching Thalmor plotline that's been simmering away until now? A load of varying endings, as Bethesda experimented with so openly in Starfield ? I'm off again. Fire up the Unofficial Elder Scrolls Pages! There's such magic here, far beyond the apparent mastery Bethesda has over theory-baiting teasers for suckers like me. These games, for instance, also have an uncanny knack for joyful stupidity. There are Oblivion NPC barks out there that landed right as YouTube's golden era hit liftoff, and in turn defined an entire generation's sense of humour. I was once in a Slack channel here called # reeblereeblereeble , which was just myself and two other writers punting Imperial Watch taunts at each other to lighten the mood every couple of weeks, or whenever someone seemed a bit stressed. When I leave a gathering of old school friends I still catch myself bidding them "farewell!" with Wood Elf gusto, and giggling at the thought of being immediately squished into mulch . And none of that is to mention the design itself, which has at times been more or less unparalleled. The clockwork, systemic magic of Morrowind is extraordinary, the first hour alone a lesson - at least as important as good old over-cited Mario 1:1 - in instructional design. Within a walkable radius of the musty little settlement of Seyda Neen Bethesda gave the player every tool necessary for understanding - and subsequently playing with, then outright breaking - its entire world. With Oblivion it brought the role-playing open world to the masses. With Skyrim it expanded what our very concept of the masses means. By all accounts I should, then, be absolutely drooling at the thought of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. But for some reason the excitement is muted. It's been like this since long before this second teaser, frankly, and for much of that time I've put it down to Bethesda itself. Bethesda Game Studios has not been on a good run. stories.title: How Long Is The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake?
stories.summary: You may think you know how long The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, but things have changed in the remake. Here's how many hours you'll need to spend with your Switch 2 to finish it.

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: How Long Is The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake?
sources.text: How long is The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time? You may well think you know the answer if you’re one of the many millions who hold Link’s first 3D adventure close to their hearts. But the remake is here almost 30 years later, and things have changed a little. So, just how much time should you put aside to finish the Switch 2 Ocarina of Time remake, and can you squeeze it in before GTA 6 arrives? We have three different accounts for you to read through, which detail just how many hours it took, and how that time was spent. I’ve spent 45 hours with Ocarina of Time on Switch 2, across two separate save files. Before I get into my time spent, I will point out that Ocarina of Time only supports one save file ! It kind of gives the impression that it supports multiple – when you start a new game, it only warns you that the five autosave points will be overwritten – but manually saving on your new file will overwrite your original file. I almost lost my 100% file this way, but luckily grabbed it from the cloud save. Onto my stats: It took me 21 hours to reach the credits, and nine more (for a total of 30 hours) to 100% Ocarina of Time. That’s every Piece of Heart, Gold Skulltula, Empty Bottle, and so on. I probably could have done it faster than this; I estimate I took five-ish hours just living in the world and absorbing all of its fine details. Pre-existing knowledge of the original is definitely an enormous help. You can rip through some puzzles, quests, and boss fights when you know exactly what to do. Then, I did it again. I started a new game and beat it in roughly 14 hours. This was mostly mainlining it – and it went fast given that I had literally done all of it just days before – but I still took some extra time to smell the roses and do some extra quests. Up next is the three heart challenge: I’ve never tried that before, but Ocarina’s lack of a hero mode makes me want to set my own challenge. For all my thoughts on those 45 hours, you can check out my Ocarina of Time review . If you take out the time I spent hunting for differences compared to the original game and riding Epona about Hyrule Field, it took me about 27 hours to fully complete Ocarina of Time. That's finishing the story and doing every side quest, alongside finding all of the Heart Pieces and Gold Skulltulas. (And spending at least half an hour doing the Horseback Archery minigame because I've always been rubbish at it.) I will openly admit to being a massive Ocarina fan, so I know this game like the back of my hand, which definitely helped in getting through it as quickly as I did. One aspect I loved about the Switch 2 remake was picking out all of the subtle changes the developers have made to the dungeons. Especially the Water Temple, for obvious reasons. Playing a Zelda game over Christmas is a tradition of mine, so I'm looking forward to a second playthrough where I'll relax and enjoy the world more. And by that I mean spend far too much time riding Epona around Lake Hylia. As our resident Zelda guides expert who has been helping readers through dungeons since A Legend of Zelda: A Link Between Worlds, I tend to take my time when going through Hyrule, making sure I’ve documented every last Piece of Heart, Gold Skulltula, and suspicious-looking rock. In searching every inch of Hyrule Field for anything not found in the original game (did you know fairies leave notes now?), my playtime tends to be a bit extended, leaving me at around 27 hours when I achieved 100% completion and beat the game. Granted, even with some of the new changes, it’s fair to say I grew up on these streets, so more often than not I knew exactly where to go and look for secrets. Still, I haven’t spent as much time as I’d like in the Hall of Fallen Foes, and I’m looking forward to replaying some of my favorite boss battles!

sources.text: I have a friend who first played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time back in the day, when the game was only just released and he was home from university for Christmas. This is objectively the best of all times to play any video game: not Christmas specifically, but dropped out of the regular world and faced with a few weeks filled with nothing pressing to do whatsoever. Years later, though, my friend told me that the magic of the game didn't just come down to the playing of it, but the way that the playing of it unfolded. Here's what he meant. He'd play all day, curtains drawn, family ignored, working through dungeons and pelting across Hyrule Field on Epona. Then in the evening he'd call his girlfriend, who was back with her own family for Christmas. She always wanted to know what he'd got up to that day. And not in East Sussex; she wanted to know what he'd got up to in Hyrule. So as he played he took regular breaks to tell someone else about what he had encountered, and what he had discovered, and what he had yet to overcome. It is my bright delight today to be able to tell you that, around thirty years later, having just revisited the game in Nintendo's new remake, Ocarina of Time is still worth telling people about. It's still an adventure so surprising, so satisfying, so moving that I need to talk about it. Here's the thing, though. Despite the game being a cast-iron masterpiece, this reaction was something of a surprise to me. Or rather, it was a surprise precisely because the game was a cast-iron masterpiece. In truth, a couple of weeks ago I wasn't really aching to head back to Ocarina of Time after all these years. I kind of dreaded having to slog through an echoing, once-great game and summon a thousand words of measured reverence afterwards. Thankfully I had forgotten two things. The first is that I am an idiot, which means that I had failed to realise that any chance to replay a Zelda should be leapt at. And secondly, it turns out that I'd forgotten exactly what kind of masterpiece Ocarina of Time is. And along with that last point - and we'll get to this properly in a bit - I hadn't realised that there's a secret ingredient to this specific remake that has proved absolutely essential to its greatness, and that has nothing at all to do with the code running on the Switch 2 . Let's deal with remake duties here. This is more or less the game that people played back in 1998. The beats of the adventure, with Link travelling between different eras of Hyrule in order to defeat Ganon, remain the same. You still start in Kokiri Forest and you still ride Epona over the fence at Lon Lon Ranch in one of the great heart-racing, skin-prickling moments in all of art. If you're stuck in a dungeon, you can almost always use an existing guide from the N64 game to work your way through it. The game world is still broken up into little chunks that fade out and in as you move between them. And each game still begins with that unskippably evocative intro that has Link and Epona dashing over a misty hill with the moon behind them, Zelda meets Susan Cooper. Changes though? For one thing the whole game's been updated with modern graphics, and has ditched any and all fixed cameras for a modern system of movement on one thumbstick and camera on the other. One example: Hyrule Castle Town, in my memory at least, always had a central camera and you would pivot about its streets as if you were a horse on a circus merry-go-round. Now it's pure Frozen territory, cobbled paths racing off in every direction and you can explore them with the camera rushing behind you. The game's spaces feel less like elaborate machines that you were a mechanical part of, and more like video game spaces. Yes, from the way I've phrased that I now see that something of a trade-off has taken place here. I loved that sense you got in early 3D games that the whole thing was a clever practical trick that was forever almost about to collapse in on itself, but anyway! The new Ocarina is a game you can show kids who weren't alive in 1998 and they will feel at home more quickly. Sometimes the graphical update is really wonderful. The route to Zora's Domain, which I barely remember in the original Ocarina, is now a lovely scramble over cliffs and arcing crags. A bold smattering of 1990s Nickelodeon colours and glossy textures, meanwhile, makes Jabu Jabu's Belly a cross between a pre-millennium rave and a modern soft play. sources.title: Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Review: Nintendo’s timeless masterpiece
sources.text: Smart updates and beautiful restorations ensure this must-play Zelda stands the test of time Thereâs something fitting about revisiting The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, nearly three decades after its original release. After all, itâs a game about growing up and watching a once-familiar world change. Like Link emerging from the Temple of Time as an adult, the scale of Hyrule Field feels a little smaller than it did all those years ago. And Iâm pretty sure the journey up Death Mountain to visit the Great Fairy was far more daunting at age 12. Yet while its environments may have lost some of their former mystique, the experience of exploring them has never felt grander. Ocarina of Timeâs remarkable Switch 2 visual overhaul, improved presentation, and more cinematic approach to storytelling give it the scale and spectacle of a modern blockbuster, elevating a story that was already among gamingâs most beloved, and making it sparkle for an entire new generation of players. What matters most, to me, is how little has been lost in translation. Ocarina of Time was hugely influential when it was released in 1998, establishing the foundation of 3D adventure games. Decades later, its world remains a pleasure to explore, its dungeons are still intricate feats of design, and its atmosphere, music, and memorable characters are nearly unmatched in Nintendo âs repertoire. Crucially, this is a remake that has been crafted with utter respect for its source material. Rather than using familiar story beats as the foundation for an entirely new interpretation, Nintendo has remained staunchly faithful to the Nintendo 64 game’s original design and tone. A handful of smart modernizations, like new controls, quest tracking, and yes, a less mazy Water Temple, make the adventure more approachable, but they donât fundamentally change how it plays. For all its beautifully improved visuals, Ocarina of Timeâs remake hasnât lost the oddness, the creepiness, or the moments of sadness that made the original game so memorable: the unsettling Mask Salesman, the traumatizing Bottom of the Well, and the melancholy of returning to Lon Lon Ranch. Itâs still very much the same strange, wonderful adventure. Only now, with the benefit of modern technology, it feels bigger, snappier, and more emotionally affecting than ever. Returning to the Nintendo 64 classic 28 years later, now firmly into my own adulthood, it’s remarkable how Ocarina of Timeâs world can feel so different, yet so much like the place I fell in love with in the late 90s. Unsurprisingly, considering theyâre the best-selling entries by a huge margin, the remakeâs young development team has overhauled Ocarinaâs presentation with Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom-style UI, including an item wheel. Like in those games, players can now jump on command, dash across Hyrule Field, and aim their bow and arrow with gyro controls. This, combined with the ability to fast-equip items like masks and boots using the D-Pad, removes a lot of the aged annoyances from the original game, while the ability to track quests via a new menu, refight bosses, summon Deku shopkeepers, and hum the ocarina tunes you canât remember the button commands for, are welcome quality-of-life additions. “For all its beautifully improved visuals, Ocarina of Timeâs remake hasnât lost the oddness, the creepiness, or the moments of sadness that made the original game so memorable” Beyond the headline changes, there are numerous smaller alterations to the blueprint for fans to pore over, including subtle nods to more modern Zelda entries. But unlike the other big 90s remakes of Final Fantasy 7 and Resident Evil 2 , Ocarina of Time sticks closely to the design of the original. This is, without doubt, the most detailed game Nintendo has ever made. The air in Kokiri Forest is thick with atmosphere, Linkâs hair blows in the wind as you cast off at the Fishing Pond, and mist stirs around your feet as you timidly step further inside the Graveyard. The remakeâs initially peculiar puppet-like characters and fairytale aesthetic soon charm you with a world that, again, feels simultaneously faithful to the original and wonderfully reimagined. Hyrule Castle Town Market is both full of familiar characters and shops, and utterly transformed, its low-res 2D backgrounds replaced with a fully 3D recreation. The fade-to-black transition to Hyrule Castle, once a blurry corner, is now an intimidating stretch of road that reveals the town extending toward the horizon, implying a renewed sense of scale, even if its extension remains tangibly out of reach. Itâs those sorts of subtle additions that bring a grander feel to the remake, despite the fact that most of its broad designs are exactly as N64 players will remember. Itâs not just the graphics that make the world feel more alive: characters bark dialogue, music dynamically changes, and the environment is more connected. The transition from the streets of Kakariko Village to its housing interiors, or Lon Lon Ranch or Lake Hylia from Hyrule Field, is now totally seamless, too, and the inhabitants of these areas will spout dialogue via UI speech bubbles – a brilliant injection of personality. Towns now follow the passage of time, bringing a little of Majoraâs Maskâs living-world feel as townspeople leave their homes to go to work, or settle in for dinner, and the gorgeous musical score is more dynamic than ever. Perhaps the Ocarina of Time remakeâs biggest triumph is how it brings a new sense of depth and spectacle to an adventure already rich in cinematic flair. Few games have used the passage of time as emotionally effectively as Ocarina of Time. Returning to familiar places like Lon Lon Ranch or Hyrule Castle as adult Link and discovering what changed in your absence remains a powerful storytelling device, and the remake’s cinematic presentation makes those moments even more affecting. “Perhaps Ocarina of Time remak

sources.text: Master Quest Remake Switch 2 The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is out November 5 in the U.S. and already live for millions of Switch 2 owners in New Zealand and other parts of the world. The good news is that the early reviews have been absolutely glowing for Nintendo’s latest exclusive. The bad news is that they’ve also confirmed there’s no much-requested Master Quest mode. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Master QuestÂ was a reworked version of the N64 game that made it much harder. It was released for the GameCube in 2003 in limited quantities around the launch of Wind Waker . Extremely rare but extremely rewarding for hardcore Ocarina of Time fans who knew the original game like the back of their hands, it functioned as a callback to the more difficult Second Quest for the first Zelda on NES. It was part of the Ocarina of Time remaster on 3DS, too . As a result, many were hoping Nintendo would include some version of Master Quest mode in the Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2. According to those who have already finished the game, however, there’s no such option here. “It honestly bums me out that the remake doesnât include a sort of Hero Mode, or even better, the Master Quest variant for veteran Heroes of Time to make us sweat a little too,” Scott White and Alex Donaldson wrote for RPGSite . Anna Koselke, in her review for Gamesradar, was similarly disappointed. “There’s no Master Quest version to play through,” she wrote. “So, for the time being, my journey with the Ocarina of Time remake ends. I’m sent back to the menu screen that still lives rent-free in my head, left wishing I could explore more of this take on Nintendo’s gem, or at least enjoy it once more without losing the mark of my previous progress.” Nintendo hasn’t been shy about delivering free content updates for its Switch 2 games. Star Fox recently received new multiplayer content, and Mario Kart 8 Deluxe even received an entire new 8-player split-screen mode on the newer hardware. It’s easy to imagine a Master Quest mode, or at least a new game+ option, being added to Ocarina of Time in the months ahead, even if it’s not clear what would stop that from being included in the base game from the jump. While players can access the original version of Ocarina of Time on Switch Online, the Master Quest add-on remains absent there as well. Maybe it’ll be added to the GameCube’s growing library on Switch 2 at some point. Donât miss the latest reviews, news and tips. Sign up for our free newsletter. sources.text: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a remake for the ages, blending the charm and whimsy of the original with more digestible gameplay and stunning visuals. It's as timeless as it ever was, managing to recreate one of the most beautiful games to date without compromising the magic of its 1998 predecessor – only adding to it. Between newly voiced dialogue, revamped dungeons, fresh puzzles, and more, Hyrule has never felt so alive. Breathtaking new visuals and voice acting Same charm of the original with changes to keep it fresh Challenging and fun without ever feeling grueling Characters and story that will stick with you long after you've played Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy. My first-ever introduction to The Legend of Zelda was my father – and, although he was always most drawn to the very old-school charm of the original 1987 NES title, little 12-year-old me fell wildly in love with a different entry: Ocarina of Time. More specifically, the 3DS release, and its accompanying special-edition console which we both spent hours browsing eBay for. I had never been so enamored by any world as I was Hyrule then. Its rolling fields, puzzling dungeons, and enchanting music had me in a chokehold, and to this day, whenever I replay Ocarina of Time on my 3DS, I can hear my dad's timely advice, smell the pine-tree scent hanging in our old car, see the Disney princess decals adorning my childhood bedroom wall… It's become less of a game to me, and more of a second home – something I find myself coming back to time and time again. No matter where I've gone or how I've grown, one thing has remained a constant throughout my life: The Legend of Zelda. From my earliest memories in Phantom Hourglass on the DS to my monthly dips back into Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom on the Switch 2 now, I always find myself in some variation of Hyrule, falling somewhere in the chaos of Link and Zelda's complicated timelines. Ocarina of Time has stood out as my most beloved journey through Nintendo's enchanting world since I first experienced it, though – and remains so. – Reviewer Anna Koselke Release date: November 5, 2026 Platform(s): Nintendo Switch 2 Developer: In-house Publisher: Nintendo That's precisely why, when Nintendo unveiled The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake for the Switch 2 , my head was spinning. Would it too feel like home? After completing absolutely everything – and I mean everything – that the new game has to offer, I'm more than pleased to report that, yes, it certainly does. It's home with bright new paint, comfortable new furniture, and one very welcome layout renovation. It's home away from home, even. You see, just enough of it is the same at its core – the characters, the story, the dungeons, the world – to be as magical as the 1998 original. But, everything that is new in the remake, from the mind-boggling vibrant visuals to fresh puzzle mechanics and more, helps solidify it as a 2026 behemoth worthy of its own place in Nintendo's hall of fame. This a remake, sure, but it's also a reimagining bigger and bolder than any I've ever played before it. The moment I boot into the Ocarina of Time remake, I'm met with the same opening menu I've seen so many times before, with Link galloping across Hyrule Field atop Epona, Lon Lon Ranch and rivers sitting in the background – except it's not the same. The detail and color almost overwhelm me. This take on Hyrule is already so alive, so much more alive than I'd ever seen it, and I've not even hit "New Game" yet. When I do, my heart instantly fills with the warm, nostalgic music of Kokiri Forest. I feel like one of the fairy children myself, enamored with the falling leaves and crystal-clear waters. I also can't help but notice the voices. Yes, voices. Saria's got one, the Great Deku Tree offers no exception, and Navi now feels like a true companion with plenty to say (don't worry, though, you still hear her good ol' classic "look!" and "listen!" remarks). I never thought that giving the cast of Hyrule a voice could make such a difference, but boy, does it. Every important figure, from the cruel Ganondorf to the Sages, now speaks to Link, helping breathe life into the once-quiet game. Each cutscene, with its new dialogue and striking visuals, immerses me into the tragedy unfolding between timelines more than the older Ocarina of Time releases managed to, and it leaves me in disbelief. The harmony between veteran devs and younger staff is apparent in how beautifully the old blends with the new. Nothing feels out of place… it's instead almost as though this is the Hyrule I envisioned as a child while playing. Our The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild review is the last time we gave the series a 5-star score, which we called "Nintendo’s finest work since Super Mario Galaxy". In my head and heart, every character had a voice – bar Link, of course – and you could see each blade of grass, each ripple in the river… and now, you actually can. The way I recall Hyrule through nostalgia goggles, albeit the way it never was, is the colorful, living kingdom it is today in the Ocarina of Time remake. The "modernization," if you will, hasn't taken away from the original's magic, it's reformed it into one just as genre-defining, but more palatable. The new magic isn't all in the game's visuals or sound design, either. It's in the gameplay. sources.text: A score of 96 puts it in as one of the 20 highest-rated games of all-time Reviews for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake have arrived with the Metacritic score placing it as the highest-rated game of 2026 but below the N64 original. Over on Metacritic, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake's score currently sits at 96 after 42 reviews, making it the highest-rated game of 2026 and beating out the likes of Phantom Blade Zero, Resident Evil Requiem, and Pokemon Pokopia. Unsurprisingly, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on N64 was not surpassed by this remake as far as Metacritic is concerned, with the original version being the sole game on the platform to have a score of 99 – making it the highest-rated game of all-time by default. However, what it has done is surpass Nintendo's previous attempt at remaking the classic adventure on the 3DS, with Ocarina of Time 3D sitting at a score of 94. In the GamesRadar+ The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review , staff writer Anna Koselke awarded the game full marks with a score of five out of five, calling it "a remake for the ages." She adds "it's as timeless as it ever was, managing to recreate one of the most beautiful games to date without compromising the magic of its 1998 predecessor – only adding to it." As far as scores go, out of the 42 reviews, Metacritic classes all 42 as positive, with 25 outlets giving it full marks on their review scales. Really, the only question now is if GTA 6 can unseat it as the highest-rated game of 2026. sources.text: Em outubro, joguei 90 minutos do remake de The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time em um evento da Nintendo na Cidade do México e escrevi as primeiras impressões aqui . Aquele texto respondeu a pergunta mais imediata: um clássico de 1998 ainda faz sentido hoje? Faz. Este é outro texto. Com mais tempo de jogo, o que interessa não é mais se o jogo envelheceu bem, e sim o que foi refeito, o que foi mantido de propósito e quanto isso custa. Eu continuo sendo estreante em Ocarina of Time. Cheguei ao fim do Templo da Floresta, já com o Link adulto, e devo estar perto das 20 horas de jogo — pode parecer um número alto, porque, sem conhecer o original, refiz alguns bosses e puzzles mais de uma vez até entender a mecânica e o timing. Em alguns trechos fui pesquisar como a versão de 1998 resolvia a mesma situação, o que ajuda a apontar onde o remake mexeu e onde preferiu não mexer. E, em 2 e 3 de novembro, a Nintendo publicou o Ask the Developer Vol. 24 , uma entrevista em quatro partes com a equipe de desenvolvimento, que explica várias dessas decisões. Boa parte do que eu tinha anotado como impressão ganhou nome e motivo ali. Mario Kart World e Donkey Kong Bananza já tinham mostrado o que o Switch 2 consegue fazer. Ocarina of Time mostra outra coisa: não é força bruta, é densidade. O ganho aqui está na quantidade de detalhe que cabe em tela ao mesmo tempo — e, principalmente, no fato de ele continuar visível nas cenas escuras, não só nas áreas bem iluminadas. Isso vale para o modo portátil e para a dock. O desempenho é estável. Em nenhum momento o jogo travou, engasgou ou baixou a qualidade de imagem para dar conta de uma cena mais carregada. É um jogo bem otimizado, no sentido mais literal: ele usa o que tem, e usa bem. Só que usar bem significa usar muito. Coloquei o console na dock com 53% de bateria e joguei cerca de uma hora. Quando parei, tinha carregado 10 porcento e o aparelho estava morno. Em jogos mais leves, com o console igualmente em uso, a recarga anda bem mais rápido — justamente porque exigem menos do hardware. Isso não é defeito do jogo nem do console, mas é uma informação prática. A Nintendo especifica a bateria do Switch 2 em 5.220 mAh, com autonomia estimada entre 2 e 6,5 horas dependendo do título, e informa que a recarga completa leva cerca de 3 horas com o console em modo de repouso . Jogando um título pesado, a conta é outra: boa parte da energia que entra pelo cabo está saindo pelo processamento. Na prática: se você pretende emendar algumas horas no portátil depois, não conte com uma sessão rápida na TV para deixar o console cheio. Ficou devendo no texto anterior, então aqui vai: está muito bom. Mesmo na tela menor, o tamanho das fontes continua confortável de ler — o que não é óbvio em um jogo com tanto diálogo. O HDR da tela é bem aproveitado, e é ali que aquela história dos detalhes nas cenas escuras aparece melhor. Jogar pelos Joy-Con não é problema para quem está acostumado. Dependendo do controle que você usa no dia a dia, a pegada é bem parecida. O porém é o mesmo de sempre: a bateria. No portátil você sente o consumo de forma direta, e dependendo da jogatina, vai precisar carregar enquanto joga. Se existe um lugar onde dá para entender por que esse remake foi refeito do zero, é lá dentro. O chão do Lorde Jabu-Jabu parece um organismo vivo. Parece molhado, parece pegajoso, e você tem a sensação física de estar dentro de um bicho. Não é textura em alta resolução: é textura com intenção. E não é só o visual que faz esse trabalho: o som acompanha, e é a combinação dos dois que cria a imersão. Essa escolha está descrita na entrevista com os desenvolvedores. A diretora de arte Aya Shida conta que a equipe não queria realismo puro: buscava um mundo denso o bastante para parecer existir, mas que mantivesse o estranhamento do original. As palavras-chave usadas internamente no início do projeto foram “clima de teatro de marionetes” e “a sensação analógica dos filmes com efeitos práticos” — duas referências que não reproduzem a realidade, mas convencem o espectador de que aquele mundo existe. O nível de obsessão é alto. Para a roupa do Link criança, a equipe pesquisou tecidos em museus e chegou a tecer amostras à mão, para que o pano não parecesse industrial — porque crianças que vivem numa floresta não usariam tecido de fábrica. É esse tipo de decisão que você sente sem conseguir nomear enquanto joga. Nos pontos em que fui conferir como era em 1998, a maioria dos puzzles é a mesma. Um ou outro ganhou alteração, e alguns mapas ficaram maiores, com uma sala a mais aqui, um corredor a mais ali. A lógica, porém, não foi reescrita. O que mais chama atenção é o que o jogo não faz. Diferente da maioria dos lançamentos de hoje, Ocarina of Time não interrompe a partida para dizer o que apertar. Não há marcador piscando, não há dica automática depois de dois minutos parado. Boa parte das soluções é óbvia; outra parte exige raciocínio e, principalmente, paciência. Um exemplo é o Templo da Floresta. Em determinado momento é preciso acionar um botão congelado. Se você ainda não fez a missão de magia — que, nesse ponto do jogo, não é obrigatória —, a saída é mirar bem em uma chama, atravessá-la com a flecha e levar esse fogo até o gelo. A mira tem um ponto certo: errou, e a flecha só queima no caminho. Exige paciência, precisão e sagacidade para pensar na solução. E, nesse caso específico, a Navi não tinha a opção de ajudar. Isso não é descuido de design, é decisão estratégica. Na entrevista, o produtor Hidemaro Fujibayashi diz que os jogos da era Nintendo 64 eram bem difíceis e que as pessoas recorriam a guias de estratégia; para este, a equipe queria que o jogador conseguisse descobrir o próximo passo dentro do próprio jogo. Ele admite, nas palavras dele, que acertar a dose de dicas é difícil. sources.text: Nintendo’s remake is comfortably the highest reviewed game of the year to date The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake has shot straight to the top of Metacritic’s list of the best games of 2026. The Switch 2 exclusive remake of the 1998 Nintendo 64 classic currently has a Metacritic score of 96 at the time of writing, based on 70 reviews. This puts it comfortably at the top of the site’s Best Games This Year page, where it has dethroned twin-stick shooter Sektori (which has a score of 93). The score is also high enough to make it into the site’s Best Games of All Time list, where it currently sits at number 24 at the time of writing. Sitting at number 1 on this list is the original Nintendo 64 version of Ocarina of Time, as the only game to ever have a Metacritic score of 99. This puts it ahead of such games as Half-Life, Gran Turismo , Metal Gear Solid 2, Elden Ring and Mass Effect 2, but behind titles like The Orange Box, Baldur’s Gate 3 and the original release of Resident Evil 4 . Given that the games ranked from 16th to 34th in the Best Games of All Time list all have Metacritic scores of 96 â with their rankings determined by more granular calculations â it’s likely that the Ocarina of Time remake’s position on the list will move up or down slightly as more reviews come in. Its position at the top of the 2026 list appears more sturdy given the three-point gap, though of course it remains to be seen whether this will last until the end of the year, what with the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 just two weeks away now. VGC’s Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake review gave the game five stars, praising Nintendo ‘s decision to not completely overhaul the original but simply add “thoughtful modernizations” where relevant. “ The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time âs Switch 2 remake is a remarkable restoration of one of gamingâs most beloved adventures,” we concluded. “Rather than reinventing a masterpiece, Nintendo has carefully refined what made it special, creating the definitive way for a new generation to discover it and returning players to fall in love all over again.”

sources.title: ‘90s style sci-fi horror Derelikt launches Nov 13 on PS5
sources.text: Solo dev Philipp Jensen reveals the secrets behind the title, which emulates PSOne-era aesthetic. Back in 1999, gaming was good. Games that were released late in the original PlayStation generation squeezed the last drop of performance out of the hardware, resulting in impressive visuals and all-time classics whose sequels we still play today. Fast forward 26 years and we’re excited to announce that our sci-fi horror game Derelikt will make you feel like your console shed 5 generations when it launches on PlayStation 5 on November 13. Derelikt takes place aboard Von Neumann Outpost, grafted onto an anomalous asteroid discovered in Saturn’s orbit. Things are rough. The work is hard, home is a million miles away, and people are stressed out. Plus, a mysterious drone is driving everyone closer to their breaking point… You arrive as an outside contractor tasked with finding out the fate of Excavation Team Delta, who went missing on the derelict surface. What you discover turns things from bad to worse fast! The halls are dark, the systems are failing, and the survivors that you come across aren’t telling the same story. Nailing that feeling of not being able to trust those around you, while simultaneously coming face to face with truly out-of-this-world horrors, was paramount for us. The Von Neumann Outpost is well stocked with an arsenal of traditional weapons, and as you progress, you might even find a few more outlandish weapon prototypes and even alien weapons at your disposal. There are also over a dozen to interact with in Derelikt, each featuring their own secrets, and agendas. Some are useful, some are dangerous, some are doomed, and some (let’s be real, most) are all three! We wanted to not only create this horrifyingly tense world full of scary moments and fast gunplay, but also make sure to make managing resources, exploration, dialogues and old-school puzzle solving a core part of the tension experience. Derelikt is very much inspired by the PSOne-era of sci-fi horror, and it feels like a full-circle moment to be writing this today. The goal was to make it appear as if we found Derelikt on a CD-R in the dusty, long-abandoned storage unit of a defunct late-90s developer and simply ported it to modern platforms. I’m of the firm opinion that retro doesn’t have to mean crude and primitive, and I set out to create the most faithful homage to 5th generation graphics available on the market. Our game features 100% lovingly hand-painted textures and vertex colour lighting. Affine Texture warping was deliberately implemented and mitigated in the next step by dynamically subdividing the geometry – just like the most high-end games of the era did – and the game also features retro-style full-motion CGI cutscenes. This way, a delicate balance was achieved – Derelikt looks aesthetically pleasing while still conceivably plausible on period hardware. Our team made a conscious effort to implement modern game design while keeping the core feeling and charm of that era of sci-fi horror intact, including an option for players to toggle on or off effects to match their particular taste. Derelikt has been in development in some form since late 2021 and has had a turbulent and exciting development journey. We hope the game is as wild a ride for players as it has been to develop! If you’re a fan of PSOne aesthetics, warping textures, geometry, heavy atmosphere, and a sense of unease, all set in the far reaches of space, then we think that you’ll love Derelikt! We hope that you’ll give it a shot, and you can pre-order the game today for a 10% discount, ahead of release.

sources.name: Eurogamer
sources.title: Remedy revenue soars by 226% following release of Control Resonant, the developer's fastest-selling game ever
sources.text: Remedy - the developer behind the recently released Control Resonant - has released a scorcher of a quarterly financial report. It shows that following Resonant's release in September, the company's revenue surged by 226 percent, bringing in €39.6m in Q3. This performance was described as "a defining milestone for the company" by CEO Jean-Charles Gaudechon. The company reported a €0.6m operating profit this quarter, a fair leap upwards from the €16.4m loss from this time last year. There are some interesting highlights to this sudden surging performance. For one, the US made up nearly half of Control Resonant's players across PC and console, followed by Chinese-speaking regions and then the UK. Perhaps most crucially is that nearly half of Control Resonant's players were entirely new to the franchise, with the company stating: "Reaching new players was a key goal for this game, and these early results indicate a growing audience for the franchise and for Remedy." Control (2019) also saw a bump up in sales thanks to the release of Control Resonant, showing a stronger performance this quarter than the past two quarters this year as well as its comparison period (this quarter last year). Remedy's CEO now believes the focus for the studio is to "get Resonant into the hands of more players." He continues to say the game has provided a solid foundation for growth as other projects (including the Max Payne 1 & 2 remake) are in the works. In short, things appear to be looking rather good for Remedy. Control Resonant was an artistically impressive but critically divisive game. While many praised the series' adventure into third person action, some felt it had less of a narrative bite than its predecessor . Nonetheless the game quickly blasted past one million sales after launch .

sources.name: PC Gamer
sources.title: Control Resonant is Remedy's fastest-selling game to date, tripling the studio's quarterly revenue
sources.text: Countless sickos of a certain vintage just breathed sighs of relief. It's been a good few months for Remedy Entertainment. In its latest financial results , the Finnish game developer announced that its third quarter revenue had more than tripled to €39.6 million ($44.3 million) from the €12.2 million ($13.7 million) it made during the same quarter last year. That spike in income is all thanks to preorders and launch sales of Control Resonant—of which only the first seven days of sales were counted in Remedy's third quarter figures. On October 15, Resonant sold its millionth copy, making it the fastest-selling game in Remedy history. "This is our first self-published game of this scale, built on our own Control IP," said Remedy CEO Jean-Charles Gaudechon, who was appointed to the position earlier this year . "Praised by players and critics alike, it marks a defining milestone for the company." Gaudechon also noted that "close to 50%" of Resonant players were Control newcomers, indicating the sequel had achieved "a key goal" of expanding the audience for Remedy's brand of stylish interdimensional sicko content. Its mission for the immediate future, the CEO said, is to continue delivering Resonant to more interested players—2.4 million of whom still have yet to turn their wishlists into purchases, according to Remedy data. "Our priority now is to get Control Resonant into the hands of more players. Excellent player reviews, penetration in all our target markets and a substantial outstanding wishlist base give a solid foundation for the game's longer-term sales potential, supported by both organic visibility as well as our targeted marketing activities," Gaudechon said. "As with the launch, we will invest with discipline, prioritizing actions with a clear return." While Remedy's operating profit margin was still thin for the quarter—1.5% of revenue, or €0.6 million—Resonant's strong launch performance is a welcome change of pace from where the studio was at the end of last year. In November 2025, it had posted an operating loss of €16.4 million thanks to the flop of FBC Firebreak. From the sounds of it, Remedy's aiming to continue that momentum with whatever work it has planned next. "Alongside the launch of Control Resonant, our other projects are proceeding in the pipeline," Gaudechon said. "Sales over the remainder of the year will ultimately define our financial year 2026. Control Resonant gives us a solid foundation for growth." sources.name: Eurogamer
sources.title: It looks like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 had fewer active players at launch in the US compared to last year's Black Ops 7
sources.text: It's been speculated for a while that Call of Duty may be losing its lustre. Although we don't have concrete data with detailed statistics for each game released in the last several years, there's an observable trend in player numbers that's hard to ignore. US market analysis firm Circana published some data showing player engagement with Modern Warfare 4 following its launch, and compared them to those by Black Ops 7 . The data is based on Circana's proprietary Player Engagement Tracker, which tracks player activity in the US across Steam and PlayStation, and worldwide on Xbox. According to Circana analyst Mat Piscatella , 19 percent of players on PlayStation played Modern Warfare 4 in the week ending 24th October, compared to 17 percent on Xbox, and 4.2 percent on Steam. With the exception of Steam, those numbers are down compared to last year's Black Ops 7, which saw 23 percent engagement on PlayStation, 29 percent on Xbox, and a meagre 1.5 percent on Steam during its launch week. Call of Duty managed to land in the top 10 across all three platforms during the same week ending 24th October, per Circana . In fact, it sat just below Fortnite on PlayStation, which is a decent result. The large drop in activity on Xbox could be explained by Modern Warfare 4's lack of a day-one release on Game Pass . Black Ops 7 was the second (and last) Call of Duty to launch on Game Pass day-and-date with its premium release. Game Pass availability typically boosts player numbers , though not always sales. The drop on PlayStation is a little harder to explain, but could be a side effect of the incredibly successful Black Ops 1 & 2 ports released in the summer on PS4 and PS5 , which captured lapsed players who may have simply lost interest in modern Call of Duty , regardless of the perceived quality of Modern Warfare 4. Judging by the data we have access to, such as SteamDB numbers showing Modern Warfare 4's launch compared to Black Ops 7's and other recent releases, there's evidence this year's game perhaps isn't as popular as it could've been. Indeed, even Activision's tenor when talking about Call of Duty first weekend sales has changed. The publisher issued a single statement following Modern Warfare 4's launch, through Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, which does not even mention the game by name. "One of the most celebrated Call of Duty games in its 24-year history, and now $40bn in lifetime franchise revenue," Sharma wrote on X . "An incredible milestone. Congrats to the Activision team. And to the players, thank you for being with us." Last year's Black Ops 7 post-launch statement sidestepped talk of sales and revenue entirely, insteading praising the "great response to the quality and depth of gameplay in Black Ops 7".

sources.text: PlayStation Studios e desenvolvedores de terceiros comentam os jogos mais surpreendentes. Há 20 anos, a PlayStation Store conecta jogadores a jogos de todos os tipos e estilos, de grandes aventuras de sucesso a tesouros indies e tudo o que há entre eles. Para marcar a ocasião, convidamos desenvolvedores da PlayStation Studios e de estúdios de terceiros a refletirem sobre um jogo incrível dos últimos 20 anos que os tenha surpreendido. Não necessariamente o jogo favorito de todos, mas um que eles não esperavam gostar tanto quanto gostaram, ou que os conquistou de uma forma inesperada. Você também pode conferir a seleção especial 20 Anos de PlayStation Store , onde poderá explorar ofertas de jogos e uma curadoria com os maiores sucessos escolhidos a dedo. Agora, veja o que os desenvolvedores compartilharam sobre jogos dos últimos 20 anos que os surpreenderam: “O jogo que me vem à mente é Balatro. Embora seja baseado nas regras simples e familiares do pôquer, fiquei completamente fascinado com a sensação de satisfação que vem de ver suas pontuações aumentarem cada vez mais por meio do progresso e de diferentes combinações. É um jogo verdadeiramente envolvente que me faz lembrar por que os jogos são tão divertidos de jogar.” – Naoki Hamaguchi, diretor da série Final Fantasy VII Remake, Square Enix “Dragon Quest XI: Echos of an Elusive Age me surpreendeu na primeira vez que joguei. Tudo, desde a história até o design dos personagens e o mundo, tem um charme difícil de não se apaixonar. Sempre que o caminho à frente parecia claro, o jogo destruía a ilusão com uma reviravolta inesperada. É uma jornada heroica maravilhosa, com uma personalidade muito original.” – Jonathan Burke, Diretor Sênior de Tecnologia, Santa Monica Studio “Um jogo que eu não esperava gostar tanto quanto gostei foi God of War (2018). Ainda é inacreditável para mim que a Santa Monica Studio tenha conseguido realizar tal feito no PlayStation 4. Mas o que realmente me cativou foi a história. Nos jogos anteriores, God of War 1, 2 e 3, Kratos foi, na minha humilde opinião, definido em grande parte pela raiva e pela fúria, com pouquíssima profundidade emocional. Mas God of War (2018) mudou isso de forma substancial. Os temas de paternidade, autocontrole, ruptura de ciclos tóxicos, luto e identidade não estavam na minha lista de expectativas. No entanto, ele se saiu excepcionalmente bem em todos esses aspectos emocionais. Pouquíssimos jogos conseguiram equilibrar uma jogabilidade incrível com uma história profundamente envolvente da maneira como God of War (2018) conseguiu.” – Ramone Russell, Diretor, Comunicação de Desenvolvimento de Produtos e Estrategista de marca no San Diego Studio “Eu não estava preparado para Inscryption. Eu achava que era só um jogo de tabuleiro com cartas meio sinistro, mas resolvi experimentar porque, normalmente, adoro esse tipo de jogo. Achei fascinante e envolvente a complexidade da interação entre as cartas e seus modificadores. Como alguém que trabalha com jogos que possuem narrativas profundas e complexas, gostei do quanto o jogo confia em nós, jogadores, para desvendar a narrativa enigmática (e a mecânica de jogo!) por conta própria. Inscryption faz algo incrível: começa como um jogo aparentemente simples e direto, que recompensa a persistência ao revelar novas camadas de jogabilidade E de narrativa a cada passo. Isso também é muito especial para mim, pois nosso gatinho que partiu vive agora como o Build-a-Card ‘lil toot boi’. Descanse em paz, amiguinho.” – Arne Meyer, Diretor de Cultura e Comunicação, Naughty Dog “Inside, da Playdead, de alguma forma, foi lançado há mais de dez anos. Não possui interface nem diálogos e oferece uma experiência totalmente única, sem quaisquer instruções óbvias, meticulosamente elaborada para ensinar por meio de uma ‘mão invisível’, de forma que pareça natural e sem esforço. Os aspectos visuais e sonoros refletem perfeitamente a história ambígua que faz você refletir sobre ela por semanas (ou até uma década) após terminá-la. É uma obra-prima.” – Marcus Smith, Diretor Criativo, Insomniac Games “O jogo que me surpreendeu completamente foi Sayonara Wild Hearts! Eu não costumo me interessar por jogos que tenham elementos musicais e de ritmo como parte central da mecânica de jogo. Mas assim que vi este jogo em ação, ele realmente me cativou e me envolveu com seu estilo colorido e único. Assim que me envolvi com a história, ela passou a me atrair cada vez mais para o seu mundo, bem como para o cenário incrível e dinâmico. Logo percebi que estava completamente envolvido em um jogo musical e rítmico, e simplesmente não consegui largá-lo até terminar a história. A trilha sonora incrível foi o que me convenceu de vez. Eu com certeza recomendaria este jogo a qualquer pessoa que normalmente não jogue esse estilo; foi uma experiência verdadeiramente memorável para mim.” – Bruno Velazquez, Diretor de Jogo, Santa Monica Studio “Escolhi ‘Shadow of the Colossus’, lançado originalmente em 2005 para PlayStation 2. Só com seu cavalo e sua espada, você galopa pelas planícies em busca de criaturas gigantes para derrotá-las e salvar sua amada, que está mergulhada em um sono profundo. O jogo é, essencialmente, Davi contra Golias. Severa no início, a aventura celebra a solidão heroica com perfeição, apresentando batalhas épicas, um grande feito tecnológico e uma trilha sonora que entrou para a história. Uma obra-prima.” – Nicolas Doucet, diretor de estúdio, Team Asobi “Uncharted 2: Among Thieves (2009) foi o que mais me surpreendeu quando o joguei no PlayStation 3, pois, depois de tanta expectativa gerada pela demo, o jogo entregou algo ainda mais épico e impressionante.
